mentions.quote: as previously spoken by Parāśara and also elaborated upon in the context of Manu's laws
just as it was spoken by Parāśara, so I shall tell it to you
the purification of things, according to the word of Parāśara
it has been said by Parāśara himself that one quarter of the penance is to be performed according to the rule

entities.description: The sage Parāśara, whose legal rulings on penance and purification form the foundational authority of the text.
entities.justification: Parāśara is explicitly named as the source of the penance rules throughout chapters 6–9, establishing him as the text's primary juristic authority.

mentions.quote: also elaborated upon in the context of Manu's laws
Manu has said they do not cause defilement
Manu has said these do not cause defilement
thus has Manu declared
By Manu alone, who knows all the scriptures

entities.description: Manu, the primordial lawgiver whose rulings on pollution, defilement, and penances are cited alongside Parāśara's as co-authoritative.
entities.justification: Manu is directly invoked in chapters 6, 7, and 9 as an independent legal voice whose declarations supplement Parāśara's own.

mentions.quote: one is purified by worshipping Śiva

entities.description: The deity Śiva, whose worship is prescribed as the specific penance for killing certain birds including ducks and partridges.
entities.justification: Śiva is named as the direct object of a purificatory rite in chapter 6, making him an active theological referent in the penance system.

mentions.quote: recite the hymn to Jātavedas (Agni)
By looking at Jātavedas (fire), gold, and the path of the moon (the sky)
The fire, though kindled in cremation grounds, is the all-consumer and radiant. Likewise, a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Veda, though he may consume anything, is a deity

entities.description: Agni / Jātavedas, the fire deity invoked through hymn and sight as a purificatory agent for sins involving animal killing and ritual defilement.
entities.justification: Jātavedas is addressed by name as the recipient of a purgative hymn in chapter 6 and again in chapter 7 as an element of visual purification.

mentions.quote: He who kills an artisan, a craftsman, a Śūdra, or a woman should perform two Prājāpatya penances
Brāhmaṇas are a moving pilgrimage site; indeed, the righteous are embodiments of pilgrimage sites
A Brāhmaṇa is the embodiment of all gods; his word is not otherwise
A Brāhmaṇa without the Gāyatrī is more impure than even a Śūdra
Brāhmaṇas who are ignorant of the Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī mantras, of twilight worship and the fire-rite, and who are farmers, are Brāhmaṇas in name only

entities.description: The priestly varna whose learning, mantras, and ritual authority define the operative jurisdiction for penances, purification, and dharmic adjudication in these chapters.
entities.justification: Brāhmaṇas are the central human agents throughout chapters 6–9: they prescribe penances, embody sacred authority, and their own purity or impurity forms a recurring doctrinal theme.

mentions.quote: If any Brāhmaṇa kills a caṇḍāla, he should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance
Upon seeing a caṇḍāla, one should immediately look at the sun
One who sleeps with caṇḍālas should be made to fast for three nights
On the first day, she is a caṇḍālī (an outcaste woman)

entities.description: The lowest-ranked social group in the varna hierarchy, whose very presence, touch, or proximity requires escalating penances from higher-varna persons.
entities.justification: The caṇḍāla is the text's paradigm case for extreme ritual pollution in chapter 6, generating an extensive casuistry of contact, food, water, and cohabitation impurity rules.

mentions.quote: He who kills a blameless Vaiśya or Kṣatriya should also perform two Kṛcchra penances
A Brāhmaṇa should perform the Sāntapana penance; the next in order (a Kṣatriya) should perform the Prājāpatya
A Kṣatriya, by giving five māṣas of gold

entities.description: The warrior-noble varna, positioned second in the fourfold hierarchy, subject to differentiated penance obligations and capable of prescribing penances alongside learned Brāhmaṇas.
entities.justification: Kṣatriyas appear throughout chapters 6 and 8 in ranked penance schedules reflecting their intermediate standing below Brāhmaṇas.

mentions.quote: He who kills a blameless Vaiśya or Kṣatriya should also perform two Kṛcchra penances
A Vaiśya should perform half of that

entities.description: The merchant-farmer varna, third in the hierarchy, whose killing or purity status carries proportionally lighter penalties than Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas.
entities.justification: Vaiśyas appear in graduated penance tables in chapters 6 and 7, consistently occupying the third position in fourfold varna rankings.

mentions.quote: He who kills an artisan, a craftsman, a Śūdra, or a woman should perform two Prājāpatya penances
There is no fast for Śūdras; a Śūdra is purified by charity
A Brāhmaṇa without the Gāyatrī is more impure than even a Śūdra

entities.description: The lowest varna within the dvija system, for whom penance is replaced by charity, and whose contact with higher varnas creates graduated pollution requiring remediation.
entities.justification: Śūdras appear throughout chapters 6 and 7 as the fourfold schema's lowest member, with distinct penance substitutions reflecting their exclusion from Vedic rites.

mentions.quote: there is no validity as a pariṣad (an assembly of learned Brāhmaṇas), even if thousands of them are assembled
the penitent becomes pure, but the guilt goes to the pariṣad
Four, or even three, who know the Veda and maintain the sacred fire, and who are capable among Brāhmaṇas—that is called a pariṣad

entities.description: The formal assembly of qualified Brāhmaṇas that possesses the authority to declare dharma and prescribe penances; the text devotes chapter 8 to defining its valid composition.
entities.justification: Chapter 8 is substantially organized around defining the pariṣad's legitimate membership, jurisdiction, and liability, making it a distinct institutional entity.

mentions.quote: If a cow dies unintentionally in its tethers or yokes, what shall be the penance for this unintentionally committed sin?
he should live among the cows at night and follow the cows by day
He who gives up his life for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or a cow is freed from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa
Confinement, tethering, overloading, striking, forcing through difficult terrain, and yoking—these are the six causes of a cow's death

entities.description: The cow is the central animal subject of chapters 8–9, whose protection, welfare, and ritual status generate an elaborate casuistry of penances for various modes of harm.
entities.justification: Chapters 8 and 9 are almost entirely devoted to penances for cow-harm and cow-death, establishing the cow as the pre-eminent animal in the text's moral-legal hierarchy.

mentions.quote: One who walks the same path as a caṇḍāla becomes pure by remembering the Gāyatrī
Brāhmaṇas who are ignorant of the Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī mantras…are Brāhmaṇas in name only
one should recite the mother of the Vedas
By reciting the purifying goddess (the Gāyatrī), one is freed from that sin

entities.description: The Gāyatrī (Sāvitrī) mantra, which functions throughout chapters 6–9 as both the defining marker of Brāhmaṇic authenticity and a universally available purificatory recitation.
entities.justification: The Gāyatrī appears repeatedly as the single most cited ritual instrument—both a test of legitimate Brāhmaṇahood and a direct remedy for various impurities.

mentions.quote: should perform two Prājāpatya penances, and the sacrificial fee is eleven bulls
he should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and give two cows as a sacrificial fee
should perform the Prājāpatya penance
one should prescribe the Prājāpatya…Then one should divide that Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance in four ways

entities.description: A named penance regime (Prājāpatya Kṛcchra) that is the standard prescribed remedy for killing caṇḍālas, Śūdras, and as the base unit for cow-killing penances divided into four graduated stages.
entities.justification: The Prājāpatya is the most frequently cited specific penance name in chapters 6–9, functioning as the juridical anchor for multiple categories of sin.

mentions.quote: the penance is the Cāndrāyaṇa, and the sacrificial fee is thirty cows
a cow-killer should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance
Their vow, such as the Kṛcchra or Cāndrāyaṇa, should be performed in the midst of their relatives

entities.description: A lunar penance (the Cāndrāyaṇa vow) prescribed for killing Vaiśyas devoted to duty, and by Manu's authority for cow-killing, representing a severe extended vow.
entities.justification: The Cāndrāyaṇa appears in both chapter 6 (for killing a meritorious Vaiśya) and chapter 9 (for cow-killing per Manu), marking it as a heavy-penance category.

mentions.quote: he who, having committed cow-killing in this world, wishes to conceal it, goes to the terrible hell called Kālasūtra, without a doubt

entities.description: Kālasūtra, a named hell realm to which the concealer of cow-killing is condemned, representing the text's most explicit eschatological sanction.
entities.justification: Kālasūtra is the only named hell mentioned in this window, attached specifically to the concealment of cow-killing, marking it as the most severe eschatological threat.

mentions.quote: he is purified…by consuming pañcagavya
fasting for one night and consuming pañcagavya
using pañcagavya

entities.description: Pañcagavya (the five cow-products: milk, curd, clarified butter, urine, dung), a composite purificatory substance prescribed repeatedly in chapters 6–7 for defilement of various kinds.
entities.justification: Pañcagavya appears in three distinct chapters as the canonical ritual remedy for contact pollution, reflecting its central role in the text's purity pharmacopoeia.

mentions.quote: it indeed has the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice

entities.description: The Agniṣṭoma Soma sacrifice, invoked as the merit-standard against which the blessing of a Brāhmaṇa ('May it be without flaw') is measured.
entities.justification: The Agniṣṭoma is cited in chapter 6 as the supreme sacrificial benchmark for measuring the efficacy of a Brāhmaṇa's benediction.

mentions.quote: For killing a curlew, a flamingo, a swan…one becomes pure by fasting for a day and a night
For the killing of an elephant, a horse, a buffalo, or a camel, the penance is to fast for a day and a night
One who kills a deer, a monkey, a lion, a leopard, or a tiger is purified in three nights

themes.justification: Chapter 6 opens with an exhaustive taxonomy of animals (birds, reptiles, mammals, predators) each assigned a specific penance, establishing graduated atonement as the chapter's organizing principle.

mentions.quote: Upon seeing a caṇḍāla, one should immediately look at the sun. Upon touching a caṇḍāla, one must bathe with one's clothes on
Having drunk water from a well that has been touched by the vessel of a caṇḍāla, one attains purity in three nights by consuming barley gruel mixed with cow's urine
One who sleeps with caṇḍālas should be made to fast for three nights

themes.justification: Chapters 6 and 7 develop a detailed casuistry in which even momentary contact—visual, tactile, alimentary, or spatial—with caṇḍālas generates graduated defilement requiring graduated remediation.

themes.topic: Brahminic authority as the sole legitimate source of dharmic adjudication

mentions.quote: A Brāhmaṇa is the embodiment of all gods; his word is not otherwise
What four, or even three, who are masters of the Veda declare—that should be known as dharma, and not what is said by thousands of others
Whatever dharma those who are deluded by darkness…may declare—that sin, becoming a hundredfold, falls upon its speakers

themes.justification: Chapter 8 is centrally devoted to the thesis that dharmic authority is not democratic but qualitative: only Veda-knowing Brāhmaṇas constitute a valid pariṣad, and false adjudicators absorb the sin they wrongly assign.

themes.topic: The cow as sacred being requiring active protection

mentions.quote: Whether it is hot, raining, or cold…he should not protect himself without first protecting the cow to the best of his ability
He who gives up his life for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or a cow is freed from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa
When cows or bulls are in peril, all the people who are onlookers and do not intervene—all of them incur the sin

themes.justification: Chapters 8–9 treat the cow as a morally privileged being whose welfare supersedes that of the penitent himself; even bystander inaction at a cow's peril is sinful.

themes.topic: Purification of material objects and substances

mentions.quote: The purification of wooden vessels is desired through shaving them
Bronze is purified by ash; copper is purified by an acidic substance
Ivory, bone, and horn, as well as silver and gold vessels, and vessels of gems and stone—these one should wash with water

themes.justification: Chapter 7 is explicitly titled the purification of things (dravyaśuddhiḥ) and catalogues material-specific purification methods, extending the text's purity system beyond persons to the built and natural environment.

themes.topic: Concealment of sin as aggravating factor

mentions.quote: He who, having committed cow-killing in this world, wishes to conceal it, goes to the terrible hell called Kālasūtra
one should make one's sin public and always practice one's own dharma

themes.justification: Chapter 9 closes with an explicit warning that concealment—not the act itself—triggers the most severe eschatological punishment, implying a doctrine of voluntary disclosure as mitigating.

mentions.quote: For a woman, there is no shaving of the hair, no sleeping and eating in a distant place
For women, there is no wearing of an antelope skin; they should simply perform the vow
Their vow, such as the Kṛcchra or Cāndrāyaṇa, should be performed in the midst of their relatives

themes.justification: Chapter 9 implicitly articulates a gender-differentiated penance code in which women are exempt from the physically arduous and socially exposed elements (head-shaving, dwelling outside, cattle-following) while retaining the vow's substance.

themes.topic: Menstrual pollution and the timing of marriage

mentions.quote: He who does not give his daughter in marriage when she has reached her twelfth year
her ancestors themselves drink her menstrual blood month after month
On the first day, she is a caṇḍālī (an outcaste woman); on the second, a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa

themes.justification: Chapter 7 introduces a distinct sub-topic—the ritual danger of delayed marriage and the symbolic pollution scale applied to the menstruating unmarried woman—as a subset of the broader purity system.

citations.quote: as previously spoken by Parāśara and also elaborated upon in the context of Manu's laws
citations.justification: Manu's laws are explicitly co-invoked at the text's opening declaration of purpose for chapter 6, treating his corpus as a parallel authority alongside Parāśara.

citations.quote: Manu has said they do not cause defilement
citations.justification: Manu is cited by name as the direct source for the ruling that cats, flies, insects, and frogs do not cause defilement, functioning as an independent authority on purity law.
Manu is explicitly credited with the ruling that a killer should give a substitute of equivalent kind or value, directly attributing the legal principle to him.

citations.quote: By Manu alone, who knows all the scriptures
citations.justification: Manu is invoked as the sole sufficient authority for the prāyaścitta of the cow-killer (Cāndrāyaṇa), with the epithet 'who knows all the scriptures' affirming his juristic supremacy.
